helpCenter.content:
The UK Employment Rights Act 2025 introduces two major unfair dismissal (UD) changes in Great Britain (GB) effective January 1, 2027: employees qualify for UD protection sooner, and the financial ceiling on compensation is removed. Together, these changes may affect how customers plan and manage termination decisions once a team member reaches the new qualifying threshold.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Who is impacted?

These rules apply to team members based in Great Britain (England, Wales, and Scotland).

Northern Ireland is not covered by the Employment Rights Act 2025 changes described below and continues to follow its own UD rules (see Northern Ireland: summary and FAQs below).

What changes in Great Britain (effective January 1, 2027)?

Unfair dismissal protection starts at 6 months (not 2 years)

Historically, employees needed 2 years’ continuous service before they could bring an unfair dismissal claim in GB. From January 1, 2027, that qualifying period reduces to 6 months’ continuous employment.

In practical terms, this makes the first six months of employment a critical period. If an employee reaches the 6‑month point, they can bring an unfair dismissal claim if their employment is terminated (including by non-renewal of a fixed-term contract), and dismissals and non-renewals will generally need:

  • a potentially fair reason—under UK law these are capability (including performance and ill health), conduct, redundancy, statutory illegality, or some other substantial reason (SOSR); and
  • a fair process in line with the ACAS Code of Practice, for example, appropriate investigation and meetings tailored to the circumstances. The steps will vary depending on the reason for dismissal—for example, performance, disciplinary, or redundancy cases will follow different processes.

Why this matters now: Any team member who has reached 6 months' continuous service by January 1, 2027 — whether an upcoming hire, a recent hire, or an existing team member — will qualify for unfair dismissal protection from that date. For existing team members, this may not have been anticipated at the time of hire and may not have been taken into account in any probationary period, probationary period extension, or fixed-term employment agreement.

If an offboarding is being considered, customers should contact Remote for guidance before taking any steps.

The compensation cap is removed

Prior to January 1, 2027, compensatory awards for unfair dismissal are subject to a “dual cap”: the lower of 52 weeks’ gross pay or a statutory limit (for example, £123,543 from April 2026).

From January 1, 2027, those limits are abolished in GB. Tribunals can assess compensation based on the employee’s actual financial loss, with no fixed upper limit. Depending on the facts, this can include salary, bonus, commission, benefits, pension loss, equity-related loss, and any other financial losses that flow from the dismissal—with no cap on the total amount that can be awarded.

Because compensation is assessed on actual financial loss with no upper limit, a higher or more complex package directly increases the size of any potential compensation.

What does this mean in practice?

For team members based in Great Britain, the key practical implication is that unfair dismissal protection will start much sooner once the law takes effect.

  • From January 1, 2027, dismissals and non-renewals at or after 6 months' continuous service will generally need a potentially fair reason and a fair process.
  • The removal of the compensation cap means the financial exposure from an unfair dismissal finding is uncapped. This is particularly relevant where a team member has a higher or more complex compensation package.

Note that other claims like discrimination or whistleblowing can arise regardless of length of service and are not affected by these changes.

Customers considering any offboarding should contact Remote for guidance before taking any steps regardless of the team member's length of service.

Northern Ireland: summary

Northern Ireland is not part of Great Britain and is not covered by the GB legislation described above. Under current Northern Ireland rules:

  • employees gain unfair dismissal protection after 1 year of continuous employment; and
  • the compensation cap remains in place (£123,785 as of April 2026; statutory limits change annually).

In Northern Ireland, even though the qualifying period is 1 year of continuous employment, once an employee qualifies, dismissals and non-renewals will generally need:

  • a potentially fair reason. Similar to Great Britain, these are capability (including performance and ill health), conduct, redundancy, statutory illegality, or some other substantial reason (SOSR); and
  • a fair process. In Northern Ireland, employers must follow a statutory 3-step dismissal procedure: (1) set out in writing what the employee is alleged to have done and what action is being considered; (2) hold a meeting to discuss it and give the employee the opportunity to respond; and (3) offer a right of appeal. Additional requirements will vary depending on the reason for dismissal.

Frequently Asked Questions - FAQs

What counts as a fair reason for dismissal?

Under UK law (both Great Britain and Northern Ireland), a dismissal can only be fair if there is a potentially fair reason. These are: capability (including performance and ill health), conduct, redundancy, statutory illegality, or some other substantial reason (SOSR). Even where a fair reason exists, the dismissal must also follow a fair process appropriate to the circumstances.

Does having a probationary period protect against unfair dismissal claims?

No. A contractual probation period does not remove or replace the statutory unfair dismissal right. Once a team member reaches 6 months' continuous service (from January 1, 2027), they will qualify for unfair dismissal protection regardless of whether they are still within a probationary period. This means that if a probationary period runs to or beyond 6 months, the team member may be able to bring an unfair dismissal claim if their employment is terminated (including at the end of probation), and any termination will require a potentially fair reason and a fair process. Notice periods also need to be factored in when considering timing. Customers should contact Remote before taking any action during or at the end of a probationary period.

Does this apply to the whole UK?

No. The changes apply to Great Britain (England, Wales, and Scotland) only. The key changes (the reduction of the qualifying period to 6 months and the removal of the compensation cap) do not apply in Northern Ireland, where employees currently qualify for unfair dismissal protection after 1 year of continuous employment and the compensation cap remains in place. The requirement for a potentially fair reason and a fair process applies across the UK. See Northern Ireland: summary for more detail.

When does unfair dismissal protection start in Great Britain?

From January 1, 2027, employees in Great Britain qualify for unfair dismissal protection after 6 months' continuous employment. This applies to new starters and to existing employees who have reached 6 months' service by that date.

What do “continuous service” and “continuous employment” mean?

These terms refer to the team member’s unbroken period of employment (sometimes described as “seniority”). It is typically counted from the employment start date. Depending on the circumstances (including what is set out in the employment agreement), previous service may also be relevant when assessing continuous service. This matters because unfair dismissal protection applies after 6 months’ continuous service in Great Britain and 1 year in Northern Ireland.

If I’m using a fixed-term contract, does non-renewal count as a dismissal?

Yes. Under UK law, expiry of a fixed-term contract without renewal can count as a dismissal. If the employee has reached the qualifying threshold, unfair dismissal rules may apply at expiry.

For employees in Great Britain, the contract end date must fall before the employee reaches 6 months' continuous service. For example, a contract starting July 2 reaches the 6-month threshold on January 1; the end date should be set before that date.

For employees in Northern Ireland, the same applies at the 1-year threshold. A contract starting July 2 reaches 1 year on July 1 the following year—the end date should be set before that date.

Do I need to have a reason for a fixed-term contract?

A fixed-term contract expiring without renewal counts as a dismissal. There is no general legal requirement to state a reason for using a fixed-term contract, but documenting the business context for why the role is time-limited is good practice. This can help ensure the contract accurately reflects the intended temporary arrangement. In Remote’s platform, customers will be asked to provide a reason for the fixed-term contract, and this will be included directly in the employment agreement. This is particularly important in Great Britain from January 1, 2027, when employees gain unfair dismissal protection after 6 months’ continuous employment. In Northern Ireland, the qualifying period is 1 year of continuous employment. If the employee has unfair dismissal rights at the point of non-renewal, the employer may need to show a fair reason and follow an appropriate process. The fair reason will depend on the circumstances.

To avoid misunderstandings, it’s common for fixed-term contracts to set out:

  • the business reason (for example, cover or a time-limited project);
  • what triggers the end of the contract (for example, a return date or project end date); and
  • the notice provisions that apply (if relevant).

Some common example reasons are:

  1. Covering a permanent employee’s absence (e.g. maternity, paternity, or long-term sick leave)
  2. Completing a specific project with a defined end date
  3. Seasonal or temporary increase in workload
  4. Role funded by a grant or time-limited external funding
  5. Temporary cover while a recruitment process is ongoing
  6. Work tied to a specific client contract with a defined end date
  7. Time-limited budget or headcount approval

Note: repeated renewals or a long series of fixed-term contracts may mean the arrangement should be reviewed to confirm a fixed-term contract remains appropriate. Contact Remote for guidance before renewing multiple times.

helpCenter.content:
How this affects your probation choice:

A probation period gives both parties time to assess whether the role and the hire are a good fit. However, setting a probation period does not prevent an employee from bringing an unfair dismissal claim once they reach the qualifying period of service — a fair reason and a fair process would be needed to end employment.

Important: Notice periods extend continuous service, so probation must end early enough that any notice served runs before the unfair dismissal threshold is reached.
 

England, Wales, and Scotland (Great Britain)

From January 1, 2027, unfair dismissal protection applies at 6 months' continuous service with uncapped compensation.

For indefinite contracts: We recommend an initial probation period of 4 months to retain the option of a true probationary dismissal. This gives you time to assess performance, make decisions and serve notice before the 6-month threshold. 5 months leaves limited leeway for decision-making, extensions, and notice before that threshold is reached.

For fixed-term contracts: A probation period should be proportionate to the length of the contract. We recommend up to 50% of the contract duration, capped at 4 months maximum to retain the option of a true probationary dismissal. Probation must end with enough time for any notice period to run before the 6-month threshold is reached.
 

Northern Ireland

Unfair dismissal protection applies at 1 year's continuous service.

For indefinite contracts: We recommend an initial probation period of 6 months to retain the option of a true probationary dismissal. This is considered reasonable for assessing the role and new hire. Probation longer than 6 months is unlikely to be viewed as reasonable.

For fixed-term contracts: A probation period should be proportionate to the contract length. We recommend up to 50% of the contract duration, capped at 6 months.

For background, see our Help Center article on unfair dismissal changes in Great Britain.

helpCenter.callToAction: Learn more about exposure and liability
helpCenter.content:
Higher salary, bonus, commission and equity – managing your exposure

Until January 1, 2027, unfair dismissal awards are capped at the lower of £123,543 or 52 weeks' gross pay. From January 1, 2027, that cap is removed in Great Britain. Compensation is assessed on actual financial loss — salary, bonus, commission, benefits, pension loss and equity-related loss — with no upper limit. A higher or more complex package means a larger potential award.

As your employer of record, Remote is the legal employer. Even where bonus, commission or equity is agreed directly between you and the employee rather than through Remote, it can still form part of an unfair dismissal claim if linked to the employment relationship. A bonus described as discretionary can still be treated as recoverable loss, commission on pipeline deals at the time of termination can form part of a financial loss claim, and equity plan provisions designed to exclude equity-related loss on termination may no longer provide reliable protection.

To manage exposure:

  • Keep probation short (3–4 months, maximum 5) to retain the option of a true probationary dismissal before the 6-month threshold;
  • Ensure bonus and commission plans are precisely drafted — defining when amounts are earned, how leavers are treated, and the scope of any discretion;
  • Ensure equity grant documents are clear on treatment at termination — vesting schedule, lapse provisions, and any leaver clauses;
  • Seek independent legal advice on any plan before it is put in place;
  • Contact Remote early if a separation may be required — settlement agreements are often the most effective way to manage liability cleanly.

For background, see our Help Center article on unfair dismissal changes in Great Britain.

helpCenter.callToAction: Learn more about contract types in the UK
helpCenter.content:
How this affects your contract choice: 

Great Britain (England, Wales and Scotland) – unfair dismissal changes 

From January 1, 2027, employees in Great Britain qualify for unfair dismissal protection at 6 months’ continuous service (down from 2 years). The compensation cap (see below) is also removed - awards will reflect actual financial loss with no upper limit. Any termination on or after 6 months (including fixed term expiry) will require a fair reason and a fair process.

Before January 1, 2027, qualifying period is 2 years; compensation capped at the lower of £123,543 or 52 weeks’ gross pay.

  • Indefinite contract: An indefinite contract has no planned end date. We recommend a 4 month probation period (max 5 months) to retain the option of a true probationary dismissal if needed before the 6-month threshold.
  • Fixed term contract: A fixed-term contract ends on a set date. If you want the contract to end automatically on expiry (without needing a fair reason or process), keep the total duration just under 6 months - including any renewals or extensions. If the employee reaches 6 months or more of continuous service, unfair dismissal protections apply and ending the contract will require a fair reason and fair process.

Northern Ireland – no change

In Northern Ireland, employees gain unfair dismissal protection at 1 year's continuous service and compensation is capped.

  • Indefinite contract: An indefinite contract has no planned end date. We recommend a probation period of 6 months.
  • Fixed term contract: A fixed-term contract ends on a set date. To rely on expiry alone, keep the total duration including any renewals or extensions to just under 1 year. Set probation at up to 50% of the contract duration, up to a maximum of 6 months.

helpCenter.callToAction: Learn more about equity management at Remote
helpCenter.content:
Remote Equity is a lightweight compliance tool designed to help you manage equity grants across borders for team members hired through Remote's Employer of Record (EOR).

Whether you’re managing vesting, reporting exercises, or navigating local tax laws, Remote Equity gives you the structure to stay compliant, avoid risk, and support your team across borders.

Why it matters

As your EOR, Remote is legally responsible for equity-related tax and reporting in the countries where your team members are employed. That means we don’t just track equity, we:

  • Withhold and report taxes when required
  • File with local tax authorities
  • Support team members with clear guidance on their tax responsibilities

Most equity platforms can’t do that because they’re not the legal employer. Remote Equity ensures we have the data we need, when we need it, to keep your company compliant and your team fairly rewarded.

Behind the scenes, our tax team:

  • Handles tax withholdings when taxable events occur
  • Provides guidance to you and your team, even when no withholding is required
  • Manages additional reporting where local laws demand it

See also: What types of equity grants should I declare in Remote Equity?

What’s included

Remote Equity provides:

  • Tracking and alerts for events that may create a tax obligation (like vesting or exercising)
  • Automated compliance reminders based on local deadlines and regulations
  • Localized guidance for team members, shared through the Remote Equity app
  • Support from Remote’s tax and legal teams, who handle obligations on your behalf
  • Integration with Carta and Pulley to automatically sync grant declarations and exercise information

Get started in minutes

Setup takes less than five minutes. Just log in to your Remote account, and launch the Equity App to follow the setup steps.

Helpful guides to get started:

  • How can I access Remote Equity?
  • How do I declare a grant?
  • How can my team access their equity information?
  • What happens if I already declared equity before using Remote Equity?

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Who needs to use Remote Equity?

Any Remote customer granting equity to a team member hired through Remote’s EOR must use Remote Equity to meet local compliance requirements.

Why can’t we just use our own equity tool?

Traditional equity tools track grants and vesting, but they don't file taxes, withhold contributions, or report income to local authorities. Remote, as the legal employer, is responsible for these actions. Remote Equity ensures those obligations are covered.

What happens if we don’t use it?

If Remote doesn’t receive timely and accurate equity data, required filings may be missed. This can result in compliance risks, unexpected tax liabilities, and issues for both your company and your team members.

How much does Remote Equity cost?

Remote Equity costs 39 USD per month for each EOR team member with equity. Learn more.

For comprehensive information, visit the Remote Equity hub.

probation_length_recommended.description: A probation period gives both parties time to assess the role. They’re not legally required, but we recommend including one. Without it, some employment processes (like background checks) can be affected.
probation_length_recommended.title: Probation period

helpCenter.content:
A probationary period is a set time for an employer to assess a new employee's suitability for the role. It allows the employer to evaluate the employee's capability, skills, performance, attendance, and conduct.

Using a probationary period can make it simpler to end employment and notice periods are often shorter or don’t apply at all. After the probationary period ends, it is often more difficult and expensive to terminate an employee.

Please note that if a probationary period is not included and you later receive unsatisfactory background check results, Remote cannot unilaterally terminate the employee’s employment.

Keep in mind that a probationary period may not be valid if the employee has worked for your company before.

See also: What are Remote's Background Check Services?

risks_acknowledgment.title: I understand and accept the employment law risks for hiring in the United Kingdom, including those related to probation and fixed-term contract decisions, and that these new hire details can't be changed once the employee is invited.

helpCenter.content:
Great Britain

I understand and accept the risks of probation and fixed-term contract decisions in Great Britain. From 1 January 2027, unfair dismissal protection applies at 6 months' service with uncapped compensation.


Probation

  • Setting a probation period does not prevent an employee from bringing an unfair dismissal claim once they reach 6 months' service — a fair reason and a fair process would be needed to end employment.
  • 4 months is the initial probation recommendation. 5 months leaves limited leeway for decision-making, extensions, and notice before the 6-month threshold.

 

Fixed-Term Contracts

  • Using a fixed-term contract does not prevent an employee from bringing an unfair dismissal claim once they reach 6 months' service.
  • 6 months minus 2 days is recommended to keep the contract clearly below the qualifying-service threshold. Up to 2 years is permitted, but once the employee reaches 6 months service, they could bring a claim for unfair dismissal at contract expiry.
  • For probation on a fixed-term contract, probation should not exceed 50% of the contract duration (capped at 4 months maximum). Probation should be proportionate to the length of the engagement.

 

High Salary, Bonus, Commission, or Equity

  • A higher or more complex compensation package means a larger potential award in an unfair dismissal claim.
  • Even where bonus, commission or equity is agreed directly with the team member rather than through Remote, it can still form part of an unfair dismissal claim if linked to the employment relationship.
  • Written details of any bonus plan or commission structure will be provided to the team member and uploaded to our web platform, and that independent legal advice should be sought on these arrangements before implementation.
  • I accept responsibility for any liability arising from compensation arrangements.

 

Notice Periods

  • Notice periods extend continuous service and can push service over the 6-month qualifying threshold, even if notice is paid in lieu.

 

 

Northern Ireland

I understand and accept the risks of probation and fixed-term contract decisions in Northern Ireland. Unfair dismissal protection applies at 1 year's service.


Probation

  • Setting a probation period does not prevent an employee from bringing an unfair dismissal claim once they reach 1 year's service — a fair reason and a fair process would be needed to end employment.
  • 6 months is the initial probation recommendation and that probation longer than 6 months is unlikely to be viewed as reasonable.

 

Fixed-Term Contracts

  • Using a fixed-term contract does not prevent an employee from bringing an unfair dismissal claim once they reach 1 year's service.
  • 1 year minus 2 days is recommended to keep the contract clearly below the qualifying-service threshold. Up to 2 years is permitted, but once the employee reaches 1 year's service, they could bring a claim for unfair dismissal at contract expiry.
  • For probation on a fixed-term contract, probation should not exceed 50% of the contract duration (capped at 6 months maximum). Probation should be proportionate to the length of the engagement.

 

Notice Periods

  • Notice periods extend continuous service and can push service over the 1-year qualifying threshold, even if notice is paid in lieu.

salary_overview.description: We will request a reserve payment for salaries at or above £131,312.37.
salary_overview.title: Salary overview

helpCenter.content:
A reserve payment is an amount collected by Remote to help safeguard against potential large or unexpected severance costs if a team member's employment or engagement ends.

In many countries, labor laws require employers to pay statutory severance. Depending on the agreement, there may also be additional contractual obligations. Reserve payments help ensure funds are available to cover these costs if they arise.

Reserves are an industry-standard practice. Once a team member resigns or their agreement ends and all termination-related costs have been settled, any remaining reserve balance will be credited or refunded.

If a reserve payment has been made but onboarding is not completed, the full reserve will be credited or refunded. If your account has an overdue balance, Remote may first apply the reserve toward that outstanding amount.

Note: Reserve payments are required only for Employer of Record (EOR) employees and Contractor of Record (COR) contractors. They are not applicable to Global Payroll (direct employee) or users of our Standard Contractor Management and Contractor Management Plus platforms

Why would a reserve be required?

Remote evaluates several factors when determining whether a reserve payment is needed. These may include:

  • The financial exposure associated with a client’s account
  • The countries in which team members are hired
  • A client’s decision to move from 14-day to 30-day invoice payment terms
  • Non-standard employment contract terms, such as:
    • Extended notice periods
    • Guaranteed severance clauses
    • Seniority recognition
    • Non-compete, non-solicitation, or non-interference clauses
  • Consistent late invoice payments may also result in a reserve payment requirement

Why was I asked to pay an additional reserve?

Some employment agreement terms increase the potential cost of ending an agreement. In these cases, additional reserves may be required.

Currently, reserves are automatically applied for:

  • Extended notice periods
  • Seniority recognition
  • Non-compete, non-solicitation, or non-interference clauses

Other agreement terms may require additional review and could result in additional reserve requirements.

Extended notice period

Labor laws in each country define a minimum notice period for ending an agreement. If the notice period in the agreement is longer than the statutory minimum, an additional reserve will be required for the difference.

Example: The minimum notice period is one month, but you request a three-month notice period. In this case, an additional two-month reserve would be required.

Seniority recognition

A reserve will be automatically issued where two or more years of service is recognized.

As a general guideline:

  • 2-4 years of recognized seniority, a reserve equal to 1-month reserve is required
  • 4-5 years of recognized seniority, a reserve equal to 2-months is required
  • More than 5 years of recognized seniority is subject to further review

See also: 
When is a reserve refunded?
What is reserve payment in Contractor of Record?

helpCenter.callToAction: Learn more about exposure and liability
helpCenter.content:
Higher salary, bonus, commission and equity – managing your exposure

Until January 1, 2027, unfair dismissal awards are capped at the lower of £123,543 or 52 weeks' gross pay. From January 1, 2027, that cap is removed in Great Britain. Compensation is assessed on actual financial loss — salary, bonus, commission, benefits, pension loss and equity-related loss — with no upper limit. A higher or more complex package means a larger potential award.

As your employer of record, Remote is the legal employer. Even where bonus, commission or equity is agreed directly between you and the employee rather than through Remote, it can still form part of an unfair dismissal claim if linked to the employment relationship. A bonus described as discretionary can still be treated as recoverable loss, commission on pipeline deals at the time of termination can form part of a financial loss claim, and equity plan provisions designed to exclude equity-related loss on termination may no longer provide reliable protection.

To manage exposure:

  • Keep probation short (3–4 months, maximum 5) to retain the option of a true probationary dismissal before the 6-month threshold;
  • Ensure bonus and commission plans are precisely drafted — defining when amounts are earned, how leavers are treated, and the scope of any discretion;
  • Ensure equity grant documents are clear on treatment at termination — vesting schedule, lapse provisions, and any leaver clauses;
  • Seek independent legal advice on any plan before it is put in place;
  • Contact Remote early if a separation may be required — settlement agreements are often the most effective way to manage liability cleanly.

For background, see our Help Center article on unfair dismissal changes in Great Britain.
